title: Swap For Longest Repeated Character Substring
description:
You are given a string `text` of lowercase English letters. You may pick any two positions and swap the characters at those positions **at most once** (you may also choose not to swap at all).

Return the length of the longest substring that consists of a single repeated character after performing at most one such swap.

A single character on its own counts as a run of length 1, so the answer is always at least 1.

**Example 1:**
```
Input: text = "bbabbbcb"
Output: 6
Explanation: Swap the 'a' at index 2 with the 'b' at index 7 to get "bbbbbbca", whose first six characters are all 'b'. There are only six 'b's, so 6 is the best possible.
```

**Example 2:**
```
Input: text = "aaabaaa"
Output: 6
Explanation: Swap the 'b' with one of the outer 'a's, e.g. "aaaaaab", giving a run of six 'a's. Only six 'a's exist, so 7 is impossible.
```

**Example 3:**
```
Input: text = "aaaaa"
Output: 5
Explanation: The whole string is already one run of 'a'; no swap is needed.
```

constraints: text consists only of lowercase English letters
At most one swap of two characters is allowed; swapping is optional
solution_approach: Brute force tries every one of the O(n^2) possible swaps and rescans the string for the longest run, costing O(n^3) time. The optimal solution first counts the total occurrences of each letter, then compresses the string into groups of (character, run length). For each group, the run can be extended by one if another copy of that letter exists elsewhere, giving min(len + 1, total[c]). In addition, when two groups of the same letter are separated by exactly one different character (pattern a..a b a..a), the two runs can be joined by swapping in a spare copy, giving min(left + right + 1, total[c]). Taking the maximum over all such candidates yields the answer in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (26 counters plus the group list, which can be scanned on the fly).
hints: Count how many times each letter appears in the whole string; no run of letter c can ever exceed that total.
Group the string into consecutive runs. A single run can grow by one if there is a spare copy of the same letter somewhere outside it.

Also look at triples of runs where two runs of the same letter are separated by a gap of exactly one character: swapping that gap character for a spare copy merges them, capped by the letter's total count.
follow_up_questions: How would the answer change if you were allowed up to k swaps instead of one?
How would you solve it if the swap could only be between adjacent characters?
